input.rationale: The fixed execution completed and decided the question: the configuration index exposed by GetConfiguration does not identify the configuration it returns, and a membership change guarded with that returned value is applied even after an intervening configuration change, while the same change guarded with the genuine configuration entry index is rejected. The interpretation is recorded against that receipt as a violated client contract, with the one applicability exclusion and the control's scoping defect stated explicitly rather than smoothed over. The defect is already verified, but its control comparison came back unknown because a leader-only control event shared one per-node admission alias with nodes that never produce it. A successor harness adds a leader-scoped admission event so both the impact and its control are decided in the same execution, which is the only change from the verified basis.

limitations: Answered: the accessor does not identify the returned configuration and the documented optimistic-concurrency guard cannot be expressed with the value it hands back.

Boundary of the finding: this is a client-contract and concurrency-guard defect, not a consensus-safety defect. Internal configuration tracking used by the main loop comes from a different path and was not shown to be affected, and callers that deliberately pass prevIndex 0 remain unconstrained by design.

The control comparison in the retained receipt came back unknown because the leader-only control event shares one per-node admission alias with three nodes that never produce it; the control's evidence is therefore its retained operand (rejected with 'configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)') rather than a holds outcome.
One node's read was outside applicability because its returned configuration still showed 3 servers at read time, which is why it is absent from comparison 0's evaluated indices.

knowledge.statement: In a live four-voter cluster whose latest configuration entry index was 3, three nodes returned a configuration with four servers while GetConfiguration's Index() reported 0, so the reported index did not identify the configuration returned by the same call; a membership change guarded with that returned value was applied after an intervening change (entry 4 -> 5), while the same change guarded with the genuine index 3 was rejected with 'configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)'.
knowledge.conditions: Observed in one execution with MakeCluster(3) plus one joining voter through the in-memory transport, protocol 3, reading GetConfiguration on every node after AddVoter returned index 3 and then applying a guarded change; one node's read was outside applicability because it still showed three servers at read time. The values are an observed instance under these conditions, not a claim about internal configuration state.

interpretations.rationale: The registered requirement was violated by the execution: the index that GetConfiguration exposes does not identify the configuration the same call returned, and the documented optimistic-concurrency guard cannot be expressed with it. Receipt 5466e7c2853749f6849e40362a2cdf00 (completed, exit 0, tests_passed) records one config_guard_start admission per node (indices 0-3) with the reference configuration entry index 3, then four config_read results: index 4 (leader server-d2b856e1), index 5 (server-22ab50bc) and index 7 (server-ee231480) each report returned_index 0 with returned_servers 4 and known_entry_index 3, i.e. index_matches_configuration false, which is comparison 0's violation with its guard_start admissions matched at indices 0, 1 and 3; index 6 (server-df765645) reports returned_servers 3 and is correctly outside applicability because that node had not yet observed the new configuration. The impact comparison is also violated: after reading the configuration and taking an intervening change (index 8, entry 4, succeeded), the guarded change at index 9 reports prev_index_from_api 0, prev_index_used 0, rpc_error empty, succeeded true and resulting_entry_index 5 - comparison 1's violation against the admission at index 0. The control operand at index 10 shows why this is about the returned value and not about the guard: the same kind of change guarded with the genuine index 3 failed with 'configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)'. The source explains the mechanism exactly: GetConfiguration (api.go:895-903) builds the returned configurationsFuture from the atomically published latest Configuration only, so the index field stays at its zero value while configurationsFuture.Index (future.go:255-270) returns that zero to every caller, and nextConfiguration (configuration.go:228-231) only enforces prevIndex when it is greater than zero, so a client that passes the value it was handed silently loses the guard that the AddVoter/AddNonvoter/DemoteVoter documentation describes (api.go:941-957). Scope and severity as recorded: this is a client-visible contract defect - the index accessor is unusable for association and for optimistic concurrency - not a consensus-safety defect, since internal configuration tracking comes through a different path and was not shown to be affected. The control comparison in the same receipt came back unknown only because the leader-only control event shares one per-node admission alias with nodes that never produce it; I record that scoping defect rather than treating the control as confirmed, and rely on its retained operand.
counterevidence: The control operand shows the guard itself works when a genuine index is supplied ('configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)'), so the failure is the value handed to the caller rather than a missing check.
One node's read was outside applicability (its returned configuration still showed three servers), which is retained as an exclusion rather than counted as a corroborating case.
The control comparison's outcome is unknown in this receipt because of my admission scoping, so it is not used as a second verified witness.
limitations: One execution, one cluster shape (four voters, in-memory transport, protocol 3); the accessor returns the zero value by construction, but only these nodes were exercised.
The finding does not claim affected consensus behaviour: internal configuration state, elections and commitment were not shown to use the accessor.
Callers that intentionally pass prevIndex 0 keep the documented unconstrained behaviour; only callers relying on the returned index are affected.

interpretations.report_answer: 已确认的缺陷（固定输入执行 receipt 5466e7c2853749f6849e40362a2cdf00，exit 0）：GetConfiguration 返回的 configuration future 只填入原子发布的最新 Configuration，latestIndex 保持零值（api.go:895-903、future.go:255-270），因此 ConfigurationFuture.Index() 对任何调用者都返回 0；而 nextConfiguration 的 prevIndex 守卫仅在 prevIndex > 0 时才生效（configuration.go:228-231），所以调用者用 API 交回的索引做乐观并发保护时会被静默绕过。执行中：配置条目索引为 3 时，三个节点返回 returned_index 0 但 returned_servers 4（index_matches_configuration false，比较 0 违反）；在一次插入的配置变更（条目 4）之后，用以 API 返回值守护的变更仍然成功并写入条目 5（比较 1 违反）；对照中用以真实索引 3 守护的变更被拒绝（configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)）。结论：客户端契约缺陷（索引不可用于关联与乐观并发），不主张共识安全性被破坏。

scope.description: One fault-free execution on normally bootstrapped in-memory clusters: a 3-node cluster plus one joining voter, a configuration read on every node, an intervening membership change, a change guarded with the index the API returned, and a control change guarded with the genuine configuration entry index. Identical to the verified predecessor except that the leader-side events are admitted on a leader-scoped admission event.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) plus MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) merged and fully connected performs real bootstrap, replication and membership changes through the in-memory transport.
AddVoter's returned future index identifies the configuration entry the client just created, so it is the independent reference for what the configuration index should report.
The read is taken against a configuration that has not changed before the read returns, so it is the configuration the caller would want to guard against.
Between the read and the guarded change the harness performs an intervening membership change, so a correctly guarded change must be rejected.
excluded: Internal configuration tracking used by the main loop, which is obtained through a different path.
Network-transport behaviour and any transport-level effects.
Performance, and callers that ignore the returned index.

investigations.question: In the captured snapshot, is a leadership-transfer order (TimeoutNow) bound at the receiver to the current leader's authority, or can a delivered order that carries no term and whose claimed sender is not the current leader (and not a configuration member) drive a stable follower out of Follower and depose the serving leader?
investigations.hypothesis: Raft.timeoutNow is the only RPC handler that changes authority without consulting any term: it does setLeader("",""), setState(Candidate) and candidateFromLeadershipTransfer.Store(true) and responds, ignoring RPCHeader.ID/Addr and the configuration. TimeoutNowRequest embeds only RPCHeader, so no term/freshness value exists to check, while the producer only sends it after it has caught the target up (nextIndex beyond the leader's last index) - a precondition the receiver cannot verify. The Candidate run skips pre-vote (raft.go:294-298) and voters skip the known-leader rejection for LeadershipTransfer candidates (raft.go:1645-1656), so the order withdraws both disruption guards at once.
investigations.discriminator: In one fault-free, normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with a stable leader at a known term, deliver a single TimeoutNow to a follower using a transport RPC header whose ID is not a configuration member (and which necessarily carries no term), then observe the target's state/term and the previous leader's state/term for a bounded interval. Control: the same non-member sender with a RequestVoteRequest that does carry a term, but an older one, must leave the target unchanged. If the TimeoutNow leaves the target in Follower at the same term and the leader in place, the hypothesis is refuted; if the target leaves Follower at a higher term while the leader steps down, the receiver-side authority gap is observed.
limitations: The witness is one execution of one fault-free in-process cluster; it establishes the receiver-side transition, not how long clients stayed without a leader afterwards.

Safety was not violated in this execution and is not claimed to be: term/vote rules still select the leader. The defect is the acceptance of a leadership-transfer order that is bound neither to the sender's identity/term nor to its configuration membership.

Because the order carries no term, a replayed or delayed order from a legitimate former leader is indistinguishable from the witness message at the receiver; the witness does not separate those two producers.

investigations.question: Can a server in the captured snapshot hold a configurations.latest (and hence GetConfiguration) that is older than its own committed log, and how is that state produced?
investigations.hypothesis: Re-scoped after reading the FSM apply path: configuration entries never reach FSM.Apply (fsm.go:105-118), so the captured helper's FSM comparison cannot show that a peer holds a configuration entry. The remaining question is whether the >5s 'peer mismatch' seen locally in TestRaft_ProtocolVersion_Upgrade_2_3 came from a peer not having appended the configuration entry within the EnsureSamePeers window (replication lag), or from a server whose configurations.latest/atomic latestConfiguration was reset behind an entry it already holds.
investigations.discriminator: Replay the captured upgrade scenario with per-node instrumentation that records, each 100ms, whether the configuration entry is present in each log store, each node's latestIndex/latestConfiguration, and the leader's per-peer replication nextIndex/lastContact. Lag shows as the entry absent from that peer's log store (with the leader committing via another peer); an internal reset shows as the entry present while latestIndex/latestConfiguration stay below it. A decisive witness needs the entry present and latest still behind after the leader's replication has advanced past it.
limitations: No execution receipt exists for this question; the negative replay result was local exploration on a scratch copy of the captured package, not the controller's fixed-input execution.
The captured failure (peer mismatch after a full 5s EnsureSamePeers window, testing.go:733-752) is a real local observation, but its cause is not established.
resume_conditions: Resume when a harness can emit both per-node log-store contents and configuration state during a run that reproduces the >5s mismatch, or when a concrete producer of a missed configuration append is identified in source.
A reproduction must also record the leader's replication nextIndex/lastContact for the lagging peer, since the earlier local reproduction converged within 250ms and could not separate lag from reset.

investigations.question: Does nextConfiguration's AddNonvoter branch silently keep an existing voter's vote (or drop an address update), contradicting the documented contract for AddNonvoter and DemoteVoter, in a way that could let a membership change fail to remove voting authority?
investigations.hypothesis: The branch is asymmetric with AddVoter: when the target server currently has Suffrage != Nonvoter (a voter or staging server) it writes only the address and keeps the existing suffrage, whereas AddVoter replaces the entry when the server is not already a voter. Read alone this looks like a membership change that cannot take authority away.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the branch against the documented contract for AddNonvoter and DemoteVoter and against the captured table expectations for each initial suffrage. A defect requires either a documented promise that AddNonvoter demotes, or a captured expectation showing Voter/Staging becoming Nonvoter; if the documentation assigns demotion to DemoteVoter and the expectations keep Voter/Staging unchanged, the asymmetry is intended behaviour and no authority-loss claim is supported.
limitations: Source-only answer: no execution was requested, so this settles the contract question rather than any live membership-change behaviour.
The captured table expectations cannot distinguish 'address rewritten with the same value' from 'address untouched', so the exact address-update effect on an existing voter was not exercised.

investigations.question: After a configuration entry is committed, can the FSM thread's own applied index lag behind the committed configuration index in a way that makes a snapshot claim an index/configuration combination the FSM does not represent, or that silently mislabels snapshot metadata?
investigations.hypothesis: The FSM thread tracks the index it has accounted for locally and advances it only for entries that actually reach it; configuration entries are dropped before dispatch in protocol <= 2 and, when they do arrive without a ConfigurationStore, return early without advancing the index. That lag is then contained by takeSnapshot, which refuses to snapshot when the FSM index is below the committed configuration index instead of labelling a snapshot with a configuration the FSM never reached.
investigations.discriminator: Trace which log types survive prepareLog into the FSM batch, whether the apply handler advances its local index for each of them, and what takeSnapshot does with the FSM-reported index versus the committed configuration index read afterwards. A defect would require either an entry type that reaches the FSM but silently skips the index bookkeeping without a stated reason, or a snapshot that is created with a configuration index beyond the FSM index.
limitations: Source-only: no execution was requested, so this is a reading of the routing, index and guard code rather than an observed snapshot sequence.
The behaviour is described for the single-apply path; the batching path tracks the last entry in the batch instead (fsm.go:145-171) and was not differentially exercised.

investigations.question: Can shouldSnapshot's unsigned delta between the log store's last index and the last snapshot index underflow, so that the automatic snapshot condition is permanently true on a node whose log store sits below its snapshot index, and what does such a node then do every SnapshotInterval?
investigations.hypothesis: shouldSnapshot computes delta := lastIdx - lastSnap with unsigned integers and no ordering check, where lastIdx is the log store's LastIndex and lastSnap is the snapshot index kept separately. A node that recovered through InstallSnapshot sets its last snapshot index to the snapshot's index, while its log store may keep a lower index: installSnapshot compacts with min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailingLogs), so a node whose log store is below the snapshot index keeps that lower index, and the node's snapshot-aware log index (getLastIndex = max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex)) does not feed shouldSnapshot. If a run reaches that state, delta underflows and the node takes a fresh full-state snapshot every SnapshotInterval until its log store grows past the snapshot index.
investigations.discriminator: Build a cluster whose leader has compacted most of its log, let a fresh or lagging follower recover by InstallSnapshot, and then record, per SnapshotInterval: the follower's log store FirstIndex/LastIndex, its last snapshot index, whether shouldSnapshot returned true, whether takeSnapshot created a new snapshot at the same index and whether a repeat install happened. A confirmed defect needs the log store index below the snapshot index together with repeated snapshot creation on an otherwise idle node; if the log store index is always at or above the snapshot index after install, or if some other producer raises it, the hypothesis is refuted.
limitations: The witness is one bounded window (900ms, SnapshotInterval 40ms, 22 samples) on one recovered node in one cluster; it establishes the condition and the repeated snapshot creation, not production SnapshotInterval cost or how long the condition persists in a busy cluster.

The observation is bounded to the automatic snapshot path on a node isolated from its leader during the window; the receipt does not separate snapshot creations caused by a further InstallSnapshot because isolation excludes that source by construction.

The control comparison in the retained receipt is structurally uncorrelated (both nodes shared one end-event name), so the control is supported by the operands recorded in the same receipt and by the requested successor rather than by a holds outcome.
No safety or availability failure is claimed; the effect is repeated snapshot work, and snapshot retention still bounds how many snapshot objects are kept.

investigations.question: When leadership is lost while a VerifyLeader request is outstanding, can the resulting future be completed twice or left permanently unanswered, given that replication goroutines still hold it and notify it onto the shared verify channel after the leader loop has already responded to the pending set?
investigations.hypothesis: A pending verify future lives in two owners at once: the leader loop's notify set (responded with ErrLeadershipLost by the step-down cleanup) and each replication goroutine's notify map (a separate map, cleared by notifyAll at the end of an RPC). A goroutine that notifies after the cleanup therefore pushes the same future back onto the shared verifyCh, where the follower or candidate loop will respond to it a second time.
investigations.discriminator: Trace who may call respond on a verifyFuture and with what synchronisation, and what happens to a future that a replication goroutine re-notifies after the step-down cleanup: a defect requires two concurrent responders (a data race on the responded flag or a double send on the error channel) or a future that is never completed. If respond is reachable only from the main goroutine holding the run loop, and the second arrival is answered under the same stateless reject rule, the sequence is ordered and idempotent, and the apparent double completion is refuted.
limitations: Source-only: no execution and no race-detector run was requested, so this explains the ownership and ordering rather than observing a concurrent step-down.
The analysis covers verifyFuture completion paths in the captured revision; it says nothing about other future types or about respond callers added later.
The timing window in which a replication goroutine notifies after the cleanup was reasoned from the code, not measured.

investigations.question: Can an InstallSnapshot whose term is current but whose snapshot index is older than the receiving node's applied state rewind that node's applied state, and is the rewind always covered by re-application from the surviving log so that no acknowledged applied entry is lost?
investigations.hypothesis: installSnapshot performs no comparison between the request's LastLogIndex and the receiving node's own lastApplied, last snapshot index or log store range: it rejects only an older term, restores the FSM from the requested snapshot, sets lastApplied and the last snapshot index to the request's values (a decrease when the request is older by index), replaces both configurations from the request, and then compacts or removes old logs according to that index. Recovering from such a rewind therefore depends on processLogs replaying entries from lastApplied+1 out of the surviving log; if the node's log no longer covers (request index, previously applied index] - for example because it had already compacted past the older snapshot index - those already-applied entries cannot be re-applied and the rewound state persists.
investigations.discriminator: Two-sided. Sender side: determine whether a leader can be induced to send a snapshot whose index is below the follower's applied index, given that a snapshot is only opened when the leader cannot produce entries from its nextIndex (below its compacted first index) and that nextIndex only moves on follower responses. Receiver side: instrument a node whose log store first index is above the index of a delivered snapshot and record lastApplied, the FSM-visible applied index and the log first index immediately before and after the install, then whether a later commit advance re-applies the gap. A defect needs a delivered request with snapshot index below the receiver's applied index together with a log that does not cover the gap, so that the applied index is not re-reached; if every delivered request has an index at or above the receiver's applied index, or the surviving log always covers the gap, the concern is refuted.

investigations.question: Can pipelined replication leave the leader's per-follower nextIndex ahead of what the follower has acknowledged, or stall progress, given that the pipeline advances its own send cursor before any response arrives?
investigations.hypothesis: pipelineSend advances a pipeline-local next index to last entry index + 1 immediately after handing the request to the pipeline, while the per-follower nextIndex and the commitment map are only updated from decoded responses in pipelineDecode via updateLastAppended. If the local cursor were also the acknowledged cursor, a dropped or rejected request could leave the leader believing the follower had entries it never stored, and a terminal failure could stall replication.
investigations.discriminator: Trace where the two cursors are updated and what happens on the first unsuccessful pipeline response or a setup error: a defect needs the acknowledged nextIndex (or commitment) to advance without a successful response, or replication to stop without falling back. If the local cursor is private to pipelineSend, s.nextIndex and commitment move only on successful decoded responses, the pipeline aborts on the first NACK and standard replication resumes from the acknowledged index, and setup errors route to the snapshot path, then the concern is refuted for this path.
limitations: Source-only: no execution was requested, so this is a reading of cursor ownership and fallback rather than an observed pipeline failure.
The transport contract (InmemTransport and NetworkTransport pipelines deliver responses in order and close on error) was assumed, not exercised.
Behaviour of concurrent stop, removal and shutdown paths while a pipeline is in flight was not traced.

investigations.question: Can the heartbeat fast path, which processes an incoming empty AppendEntries in the transport's connection goroutine instead of the run loop, interleave unsafely with main-loop transitions such as committing a configuration entry, installing a snapshot, stepping down or starting an election?
investigations.hypothesis: The fast path deliberately bypasses the single-threaded run loop, so its safety cannot come from serialisation. It must come from two things: the request shape restricts which mutations are reachable, and every reachable mutation is taken through a synchronised accessor or a lock-protected field. A defect would need either a field read and written by both paths without synchronisation, or an observable anomaly such as the fast path adopting a term or leader that the main loop then contradicts, or a transition (step-down, election start) lost because the loop never observes it.
investigations.discriminator: Enumerate the code reachable for a heartbeat-shaped request and check each mutation's synchronisation (raftState accessors for term/commit/applied, lastLock for snapshot and log indexes, leaderLock for leader address and ID, lastContactLock for last contact, channel sends for observations), then check whether any other producer in the revision can emit an AppendEntries with that same shape while relying on main-loop serialisation. A defect requires an unsynchronised shared field or a producer that can reach main-loop-only state through the fast path; if the classification confines the fast path to the leader's dedicated heartbeat requests and every reachable mutation is lock- or atomic-protected, the concern is refuted at source level, with the residual boundary that an interleaving proof is not attempted.
limitations: Source-only, and deliberately so: the fast path exists only on the network transport (inmem_transport.go:72-76 declines it), and this run's execution isolation has no network namespace, so a network-transport execution is not available in this run.
A local race-detector run of two cluster harnesses was clean, but those harnesses use the in-memory transport, which does not take the fast path, so they say nothing about it.
No interleaving proof is attempted; the assessment covers which mutations are reachable and how they are synchronised.
Observer notification, metrics and stable-store writes reached by a term increase were read but not exercised concurrently.

investigations.question: Does the configuration index exposed by GetConfiguration identify the configuration it returns, and can a caller use that value as the prevIndex guard of a later membership change so that a change is rejected when the configuration has moved on in the meantime?
investigations.hypothesis: GetConfiguration builds its future locally from the atomically published latest configuration and never fills the index field, so ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns the zero value for every caller while Configuration() carries the real membership. The prevIndex guard in nextConfiguration is only enforced when prevIndex is greater than zero, so a caller that passes the returned index is silently unguarded, while the same change guarded with the genuine configuration entry index is rejected once the configuration has advanced.
investigations.discriminator: Read the configuration from the API on each node of a live cluster whose configuration entry index the caller learned from the membership-change future, and compare the returned index with that index; then take an intervening configuration change and retry a guarded change using the value the API returned, with the genuine index as control. A defect needs the returned index not to identify the returned configuration and the guarded change to be applied anyway when the configuration has moved on, while the genuine-index control is rejected; the hypothesis is refuted if the returned index matches the configuration entry index or if the guard rejects the API-derived value.
limitations: Native local run of the requested harness (not retained evidence) showed all four nodes returning index 0 with 4 servers visible and a known configuration entry index of 3, a guarded change using the returned value succeeding, and the genuine-index control failing with 'configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)'.
The defect is about the value the accessor reports and the guard it feeds; it does not weaken the internal configuration tracking used by the main loop, which is filled through a different path.
No execution receipt exists yet; the controller's execution is what counts.

knowledge.statement: Raft.timeoutNow performs an unconditional authority transition on the receiver: it clears the known leader, sets the state to Candidate, stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer=true and responds with an empty TimeoutNowResponse. It never inspects the RPC header identity, the current configuration, or any term, and observes no election or heartbeat precondition before transitioning.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to every TimeoutNowRequest that passes checkRPCHeader, delivered to a server in any run state; the request carries only RPCHeader (ProtocolVersion, ID, Addr) and therefore cannot be evaluated for freshness.

knowledge.statement: While candidateFromLeadershipTransfer is set, runCandidate does not pre-vote: it calls electSelf directly, which increments the current term and sends RequestVote with LeadershipTransfer=true. The flag is cleared by a deferred store(false) when the candidate run ends.
knowledge.conditions: Set only by timeoutNow in the captured source; applies to a node that then enters/continues the candidate state.

knowledge.statement: requestVote rejects a vote request that arrives while a different leader is known, but skips that rejection when req.LeadershipTransfer is true; the older-term rejection and the log-suffix comparison still run before a vote is granted.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to RequestVoteRequest handling on any server that has a recorded leader whose address differs from the candidate and whose protocol version carries the LeadershipTransfer flag.

knowledge.statement: The other authority-bearing RPC handlers guard their state change with the sender's term: appendEntries returns early when a.Term is below the current term and only adopts/updates term and state when the request term is greater (or the receiver is not a follower), and installSnapshot ignores a snapshot whose request term is older than the current term.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to AppendEntriesRequest and InstallSnapshotRequest processing; this is the control contrast for the TimeoutNow handler, which has no term to compare.

knowledge.statement: The leader-side leadershipTransfer routine only issues the TimeoutNow RPC after it has driven the target's replication nextIndex past the leader's last log index, i.e. the producer establishes a caught-up target before transferring.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the sender path invoked from leaderLoop; it is not verified by, nor visible to, the receiving timeoutNow handler.

knowledge.statement: GetConfiguration does not read main-thread membership state: it returns a configurationsFuture whose configurations field is filled from the atomically published latestConfiguration, which is written only by setLatestConfiguration (and cleared/initialised elsewhere), so the value a client sees is whatever that atomic last held.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to any caller of GetConfiguration on any server, including followers, independent of the main-thread run loop.

knowledge.statement: Configuration log entries are not delivered to the FSM: the apply loop dispatches only LogCommand to r.fsm.Apply, and for LogConfiguration it calls ConfigurationStore.StoreConfiguration only when the FSM implements ConfigurationStore (otherwise it returns early). MockFSM therefore records only LogCommand payloads in its logs slice and never records a configuration unless the ConfigStoreFSM option is used.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to commit-application in the captured snapshot for every server, regardless of protocol version; Noop and barrier entries likewise never reach FSM.Apply.

knowledge.statement: The captured cluster test helper's EnsureSame compares FSM-applied log payloads and the FSM's recorded configuration list, and its polling limit defaults to 5 seconds (overridden only by a positive MakeClusterOpts.LongstopTimeout). Built with a plain MockFSM and without ConfigStoreFSM, both compared values are empty for a scenario whose only entries are configuration and noop entries, so EnsureSame can pass without establishing that a peer holds the configuration entry.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to clusters created through MakeCluster/MakeClusterCustom without ConfigStoreFSM; the configuration comparison is only meaningful when the FSM implements ConfigurationStore.

knowledge.statement: The appendEntries truncation path is not a mechanism for configurations.latest to stay stale: on a term conflict the conflicting entry is included in newEntries, the suffix is stored, and processConfigurationLogEntry is run for every new entry in the same call, so a configuration entry is (re)applied when it is (re)appended; when the truncated suffix really contained a configuration entry, rolling latest back to the committed configuration is the intended result.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to appendEntries handling of AppendEntriesRequest batches that clear a log suffix at or below configurations.latestIndex.

knowledge.statement: Membership changes are applied with command-specific suffrage rules: AddVoter replaces a non-voter/staging entry with a Voter and only rewrites the address of an existing Voter; AddNonvoter appends a Nonvoter when the server is absent and, when the server is already present with a different suffrage (Voter or Staging), only writes its address while keeping that suffrage; DemoteVoter is the command that turns an existing server into a Nonvoter; RemoveServer deletes the entry. A resulting configuration with no voters is rejected.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to nextConfiguration for a request whose prevIndex matches the current configuration index; the capture's table expectations record the suffrage outcome for each command and initial suffrage.

knowledge.statement: Only some committed log types reach the FSM thread: prepareLog returns a commit tuple for LogBarrier and LogCommand, and for LogConfiguration only when protocolVersion > 2. LogNoop, LogAddPeerDeprecated, LogRemovePeerDeprecated and LogConfiguration under protocol <= 2 return nil, so they never enter the FSM batch; processLogs still responds to any future attached to them from the main thread and then advances lastApplied.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to processLogs dispatching committed entries to fsmMutateCh on the leader and on followers, for every configuration of the FSM (with or without ConfigurationStore and BatchingFSM).

knowledge.statement: The FSM thread's local applied index advances for every entry it receives, except for LogConfiguration when the FSM does not implement ConfigurationStore, where the handler returns early on the stated grounds of not incrementing the index for an unimplemented operation. The index it reports in a snapshot request is that local index, so it can legitimately sit below the committed configuration index.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the single-apply path in runFSM; the batching path instead takes the index and term of the last entry in the batch whether or not it was sent to ApplyBatch.

knowledge.statement: takeSnapshot refuses to create a snapshot when the FSM-reported index is below the committed configuration index, and otherwise records that index/term together with the committed configuration and its index, then compacts only up to min(snapshot index, last log index - TrailingLogs).
knowledge.conditions: Applies to automatic and user-triggered snapshots on any server; the committed configuration is read from the main thread through configurationsCh after the FSM snapshot has been started.

knowledge.statement: A server's reported last log index is max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex), so installing a snapshot raises the server's last index even though appendEntries and installSnapshot do not rewrite the stored log index; installSnapshot updates lastApplied, the last snapshot index, both configurations and log compaction.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to raftState.getLastIndex as used by election and replication bookkeeping and to the InstallSnapshot handler.

knowledge.statement: The automatic snapshot condition compares the log store's last index with the snapshot index using an unsigned subtraction and no ordering guard, so a log store index below the snapshot index makes the comparison permanently true.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to shouldSnapshot as invoked by the snapshot goroutine on its random SnapshotInterval; the log store index is the store's own LastIndex, not the snapshot-aware getLastIndex.

knowledge.statement: A node that recovers through InstallSnapshot while its log store keeps a lower index reports shouldSnapshot() as true indefinitely and keeps creating fresh snapshots at the installed snapshot index while completely idle: in two executions of the same fixed harness the recovered node produced 15 and 13 distinct snapshot IDs at index 202 with applied_delta 0 over a 900ms window (SnapshotInterval 40ms), while the leading node of the same cluster reported shouldSnapshot() false and exactly 1 distinct snapshot ID at index 202.
knowledge.conditions: Observed with MakeCluster(3), SnapshotInterval 40ms, SnapshotThreshold 20, TrailingLogs 5, in-memory log/snapshot stores, protocol 3, after isolating one follower, committing 140 further commands so the leader's log compacts past that follower's next index, reconnecting so the follower recovers by InstallSnapshot (log store last index stays 62, snapshot index 202), then isolating the recovered node for a 900ms window sampled every 40ms. Two executions are instances, not a universal guarantee; MonotonicLogStore implementations, production SnapshotInterval values and long-running persistence were not observed.

knowledge.statement: A verifyFuture can be woken by only one notification (vote is guarded by the notify channel being non-nil and set to nil when it fires), and every respond path is idempotent through the deferError responded flag; vote(true) only notifies once the counted votes reach quorumSize, while vote(false) notifies immediately so the leader loop can step down when any peer reports a new leader.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to VerifyLeader/verifyFuture handling in the captured revision, including the quorumSize==0 dispatch sentinel and the follower/candidate paths that reject arrivals on the shared verify channel with ErrNotLeader.

knowledge.statement: On stepping down, the leader loop responds ErrLeadershipLost to every future still in its own notify set; replication goroutines keep their notify maps separate and only clear them through notifyAll at the end of a replication RPC, so a late notification can push an already-answered verify future back onto the shared verify channel, where the next non-leader loop answers it again through the idempotent respond path.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to leadership loss (step-down, shutdown, or state change out of Leader) with outstanding VerifyLeader requests; the arrivals are handled by whichever run loop is active when they are read.

knowledge.statement: InstallSnapshot validates freshness only by term: an older term is ignored, a newer term transitions the receiver to follower and is adopted, and there is no comparison of the request's LastLogIndex with the receiver's own lastApplied, last snapshot index or log store range. On success the handler restores the FSM from the requested snapshot, sets lastApplied to the request's LastLogIndex, sets the last snapshot index to the request's LastLogIndex/LastLogTerm, replaces both the latest and committed configurations from the request, and then removes all old logs (monotonic stores) or compacts up to the request's index.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to InstallSnapshotRequest handling on any server that reaches the handler, including a server whose own applied index or snapshot index is higher than the request's; the only preceding checks in the handler are the snapshot version bounds and the term.

knowledge.statement: Recovery from a restored snapshot index depends on log replay: processLogs rejects an index at or below lastApplied, otherwise it walks from lastApplied+1 to the target index fetching each log from the store and panics when a needed entry is missing, so a restored index below the previously applied index leaves re-application to entries that must still exist in the log.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to commit-application on any server after a restore, including the install path that sets lastApplied from the request; the walk is bounded by the target commit index and sources entries either from the in-flight future map or the log store.

knowledge.statement: The sender reaches the snapshot path only when it cannot produce entries from its per-peer nextIndex, and nextIndex moves on follower responses: a rejected AppendEntries sets nextIndex to max(min(nextIndex-1, response.LastLog+1), 1), and the snapshot is opened when setupAppendEntries reports the log is not found, i.e. when the needed prefix has been compacted away.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the leader-side replication loop for each peer; the reported last log index used in the backoff comes from the follower's AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog.

knowledge.statement: Across three executions of the same isolation/compaction/reconnect probe on a 3-node in-memory cluster, the node that entered the InstallSnapshot path never reported an applied index below its own maximum: its applied index advanced 27 -> 112 -> 197 -> 257 across rounds with decrease_count 0 and applied_at_end equal to max_applied_seen, while its snapshot index (257) stayed above its surviving log store last index (197) and the two nodes that never entered the install path were monotone as well (snapshot index 257, log store last index 257, decrease_count 0).
knowledge.conditions: Observed with MakeCluster(3), SnapshotInterval 30ms, SnapshotThreshold 10, TrailingLogs 5, in-memory log/snapshot stores, protocol 3, in three rounds of 25 warm commands, isolating one follower, 60 further commands through the remaining quorum, reconnecting, and polling all nodes every 2ms for 1.2s. The probe does not construct a leader snapshot index below a follower's applied index, so this is an observed bounded result and not a guarantee for other configurations.

knowledge.statement: Pipelined replication keeps two separate cursors: pipelineSend advances a private send cursor to the last pipelined entry index + 1 as soon as the request is handed to the pipeline, while the per-follower nextIndex and the commitment map advance only from successful decoded responses (updateLastAppended stores nextIndex = last entry index + 1 and matches commitment, then notifies the verify futures as leader). The decoder aborts the pipeline on the first unsuccessful response, on a newer term (notifyAll(false) plus a step-down notification) and pipelineSend returns shouldStop when setup fails such as a compacted prefix, after which the caller falls back to standard replication or the snapshot path. setPreviousLog additionally special-cases nextIndex-1 equal to the last snapshot index so a snapshot-backed prefix is accepted as the previous log entry.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the leader-side pipeline path in the captured revision for peers that support AppendEntriesPipeline, including the fallback to replicateTo after the pipeline aborts.

knowledge.statement: An incoming AppendEntries is classified as a heartbeat by its field values on the receiving side (non-zero term, a leader address present, PrevLogEntry and PrevLogTerm zero, no entries, LeaderCommitIndex zero). When the transport has a heartbeat handler, it is invoked directly from the connection goroutine and the RPC never reaches the consumer channel; otherwise the request is dispatched to the run loop like any other RPC. The handler registered by Raft is processHeartbeat, which checks shutdown and the command type and then calls the same appendEntries handler the run loop uses.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to NetworkTransport (and to transports that implement SetHeartbeatHandler); InmemTransport declines the fast path and pushes heartbeats onto the consumer channel. The classification depends on request field values, not on an explicit RPC type.

knowledge.statement: For a heartbeat-shaped request the reachable mutations are narrow: the older-term check can return without touching state, a newer term or the sentinel condition sets the state to Follower and adopts the term, the leader address and ID are recorded, and success sets last contact; the previous-log check, the entry loop, configuration processing and the commit-index update are all skipped because PrevLogEntry is zero, there are no entries and LeaderCommitIndex is zero. Each reachable mutation goes through a synchronised accessor (atomic state or lastLock for snapshot/log indexes), leaderLock, lastContactLock, or a channel send for observer notification.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the appendEntries code path when invoked with a heartbeat-shaped request, whether by the transport fast path or the run loop; a request with entries, a non-zero PrevLogEntry or a non-zero LeaderCommitIndex takes the ordinary path and is not covered by this statement.

knowledge.statement: The leader's heartbeat goroutine sends a request carrying only the RPC header, term and leader fields, so its LeaderCommitIndex is zero; on a successful response it refreshes last contact, resets the failure count and notifies any waiting verify futures with the response's success value. Followers therefore learn the leader's commit index from the replicate loop's random CommitTimeout path rather than from heartbeats.

knowledge.statement: GetConfiguration returns a configurationsFuture whose configurations value is built from the atomically published latest configuration only, so Configuration() reports the real membership while Index() reports the zero value for every caller regardless of the configuration entry the value came from. knowledge.conditions: Applies to Raft.GetConfiguration on any server and to every membership change command routed through nextConfiguration; the internal configuration tracking filled from the main thread through configurationsCh does carry the index and is unaffected.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster; one control RPC (stale-term RequestVote from a non-member claimed sender) followed by one TimeoutNow from the same claimed sender to a follower, with bounded observation of target and leader state/term.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) performs real bootstrap: initial configuration entry, leader election and log replication through the in-memory transport.
Both RPCs are delivered over the in-memory transport with no packet loss, reordering or delay, so any observed transition is caused by the delivered request itself.
The sender identity in the RPC header ('ghost-not-in-config') is deliberately not a configuration member; the probe does not rely on the sender being reachable or registered.
The cluster is healthy before the probe: a leader is serving at a known term, which the harness records as steady_state.
excluded: Network-transport authentication, TLS and peer-identity properties outside the Raft layer.
State-machine safety (log matching, single vote per term) and any claim that the newly elected leader violates it.
Behaviour after the observation interval, further elections, and client-visible unavailability.

parameters.control_request_term: target term at steady state minus 1

basis.prefix: The harness builds the prefix itself with the captured test facilities: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) bootstraps a three-voter configuration through the in-memory transport, waits for a stable leader (c.Leader()), and records the leader id/address/term and the chosen follower's state/term as CA_EVENT steady_state. It then selects the follower's transport peer as sender and emits CA_EVENT control_stale_request_vote after delivering a RequestVoteRequest with Term = targetTerm-1 and RPCHeader.ID = 'ghost-not-in-config'. Only then does it deliver the single TimeoutNowRequest with the same RPC header (no term field exists) and emit CA_EVENT after_timeout_now after a bounded 2s observation of the target and the previous leader. No state is injected and no storage is pre-filled.
basis.requirement: A delivered leadership-transfer order is processed as authority to depose the known leader even though the message carries no term and its claimed sender is not the serving leader or a configuration member; the receiver performs no term, identity or membership check before clearing the leader and starting an election.
basis.responsibility: Receiver-side admission of a leadership-transfer order in Raft.timeoutNow, and the two guards that the order disables: the candidate pre-vote gate and the known-leader vote rejection.

comparisons.description: Control: a request that carries a stale term from the same non-member claimed sender is refused and leaves the target in Follower at its original term.
Probe: the delivered order moves the follower out of Follower and raises its term, although the order carries no term and its claimed sender is not the leader or a member.
Probe consequence: the previously serving leader is no longer Leader and reports a higher term within the bounded observation interval.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with a small SnapshotInterval/SnapshotThreshold/TrailingLogs: warm traffic, isolation of one follower, further traffic so the leader compacts, reconnection so the follower recovers by InstallSnapshot, then a bounded idle window on the recovered node (isolated again so no further InstallSnapshot can occur) with the leader observed over the same window as control.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) with SnapshotInterval=40ms, SnapshotThreshold=20, TrailingLogs=5 performs real bootstrap, replication, snapshots and log compaction through the in-memory transport.

Disconnecting only the chosen follower leaves the leader with a quorum (itself plus the other follower), so the cluster keeps committing and the leader's log compacts past the isolated follower's next index.
The isolated follower does not raise its term while isolated because pre-vote is active by default, so reconnecting lets the leader complete the recovery without a spurious election.
Isolating the recovered node again before the window removes the leader as a source of further snapshots, so any new snapshot in that node's store must be produced by its own snapshot goroutine.
Both observed nodes run the same configuration; the leader is idle in the window except for heartbeats.
excluded: Safety claims: no state-machine divergence, lost entry or double application is asserted.
Cost measurement: bytes written, disk wear and FSM Snapshot() latency are not measured.
Behaviour with MonotonicLogStore implementations, which take the removeOldLogs branch instead of compactLogs.
Duration of the condition under production SnapshotInterval values.

basis.prefix: The harness builds the prefix with the captured test facilities and real producers only: MakeCluster(3, conf) with SnapshotInterval=40ms, SnapshotThreshold=20 and TrailingLogs=5 bootstraps the cluster; leader.Apply() commits 60 warm commands so every node snapshots; the chosen follower is cut off with c.Disconnect and 140 further commands are committed by the remaining quorum so the leader's log compacts; c.FullyConnect reconnects and the follower recovers through the InstallSnapshot handler. No storage is pre-filled and no production code is modified.
basis.requirement: On a server whose log store last index sits below its last snapshot index, the automatic snapshot condition computes the delta between the log store index and the snapshot index as an unsigned subtraction without an ordering guard, so the condition stays true while the server is idle and its snapshot goroutine keeps creating fresh snapshots at the same index.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with SnapshotInterval=30ms, SnapshotThreshold=10 and TrailingLogs=5, running three rounds of: 25 warm commands, isolate one follower, 60 further commands by the remaining quorum, reconnect, then 1.2s of polling every 2ms that records each node's applied index, snapshot index and log store last index.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) with the settings above performs real bootstrap, replication, snapshotting and compaction through the in-memory transport.

Isolating one follower leaves the leader with a quorum, so commits continue and the leader's log compacts past that follower's next index, making the follower recover through the real InstallSnapshot handler on reconnect.
Polling every 2ms is dense enough to observe an applied-index decrease if one occurs, because an install sets lastApplied directly from the request.

The install signature (snapshot index above the log store last index) identifies a node that has been through InstallSnapshot or is in the post-install state; nodes without it are the steadier comparison within the same execution.
excluded: Configurations where the leader's latest snapshot index is below a follower's applied index, which the probe does not deliberately construct.
Monotonic log store implementations, which take the removeOldLogs branch.
Client-visible consequences of a hypothetical rewind and any performance measurement.

basis.prefix: The harness builds everything with captured test facilities and real producers: MakeCluster(3, conf) with SnapshotInterval=30ms, SnapshotThreshold=10, TrailingLogs=5 bootstraps the cluster and Elects a leader; each round applies 25 commands through leader.Apply, chooses the lexicographically first follower, records its applied index, snapshot index and log store last index, cuts it off with c.Disconnect, commits 60 further commands through the remaining quorum, reconnects with c.FullyConnect, and then polls all three nodes every 2ms for 1.2s. During polling the harness tracks each node's maximum applied index, any applied-index decrease with the snapshot index and log store last index at that moment, the number of snapshot-index changes, and how many poll ticks showed the snapshot index above the log store last index (the install signature). probe_start and one round_start per round record the scenario operands; per node the harness emits recovered_node_probe_end when the install signature was seen and steady_node_probe_end otherwise, carrying max_applied_seen, applied_at_end, observed_applied_decrease, decrease_count, the prior and new applied index and the snapshot/log index at the decrease, snapshot_index_changes, install_signature_ticks and the end state. No storage is pre-filled and no production code is modified.
basis.requirement: No InstallSnapshot delivered in this scenario moves a receiver's applied index backwards: a request whose snapshot index is below the receiver's applied state would show up as an applied-index decrease with the snapshot index below the previously observed applied index, and the receiver's applied index must stay monotone across the isolation, compaction and recovery rounds.
basis.responsibility: Receiver-side admission and applied-state bookkeeping of InstallSnapshot (lastApplied set from the request, snapshot index, log store range) observed through the values the node reports while the leader drives real installs.

comparisons.description: Recovered node: having been through the install path during the rounds, its applied index never moved backwards, so no delivered snapshot was older than its applied state in this execution.

Same-execution comparison: nodes that never showed the install signature kept applied state monotone as well, so a decrease would have to be attributed to the install path rather than to polling or snapshotting in general.

interpretations.rationale: The lag is real but contained, and the containment is explicit rather than accidental. Committed entries reach the FSM thread only if prepareLog builds a tuple for them (raft.go:1362-1387): LogBarrier and LogCommand always, LogConfiguration only when protocolVersion > 2, while LogNoop and the deprecated peer entries return nil and are never dispatched; processLogs (raft.go:1292-1358) responds to their futures itself and then advances lastApplied. Inside the FSM thread (fsm.go:92-125) every received entry advances the local lastIndex/lastTerm except a LogConfiguration when the FSM does not implement ConfigurationStore, which returns early with the explicit reason that the index should not advance for an unimplemented operation. The snapshot request reports that local index (fsm.go:216-233), so after a committed configuration change with no later command or barrier the FSM index can sit below the committed configuration index. takeSnapshot (snapshot.go:125-211) reads the committed configuration from the main thread afterwards and refuses to snapshot when snapReq.index < committedIndex, with a comment naming exactly this case, so metadata is never labelled with a configuration the FSM has not reached; compaction is separately bounded by min(snapshot index, last log index - TrailingLogs) (snapshot.go:213-240), so nothing beyond the log's last index is trimmed. interpretations.rationale: The apparent double completion is refuted by completion ownership and ordering. verifyLeader registers the future in the leader loop's notify set and in each replication goroutine's notify map, and the step-down cleanup responds ErrLeadershipLost to everything still in the leader's own set (raft.go:511-526). The replication maps are separate and are only cleared by notifyAll when an RPC finishes (replication.go:100-111), so a goroutine that finishes its heartbeat after the cleanup can still call vote on the same future; vote sends the future onto the shared verify channel and nils its notify channel under voteLock, so it wakes at most once (future.go:272-293). The critical point is who responds: respond is reachable only from the main run loop for this future type (the leader loop's verify branch, the follower and candidate reject branches, and the step-down cleanup), and all of those execute on the single main goroutine, so the cleanup's respond and any later rejection are sequentially ordered rather than concurrent. The second arrival is therefore a no-op: deferError.respond returns early once responded is set, and if it were reached first it would simply answer ErrNotLeader through the same idempotent path (future.go:94-131, raft.go:181-186). The result is that a VerifyLeader outstanding at leadership loss is answered exactly once - ErrLeadershipLost from the cleanup - and any late wake-up on the shared channel is swallowed by the responded flag instead of double-closing the error channel or blocking a sender. A worthwhile boundary follows from the same reading but is not a defect: because vote records a false reply immediately, the leader steps down and answers ErrNotLeader as soon as a single peer reports a new leader, and because votes are only counted from replies, a partition that silences peers leaves the request unanswered until a reply, shutdown or the caller's own timeout resolves it.

Control: the same non-member sender with a RequestVoteRequest that does carry a term, but an older one, must leave the target unchanged. If the TimeoutNow leaves the target in Follower at the same term and the leader in place, the hypothesis is refuted; if the target leaves Follower at a higher term while the leader steps down, the receiver-side authority gap is observed.

Safety was not violated in this execution and is not claimed to be: term/vote rules still select the leader. The defect is the acceptance of a leadership-transfer order that is bound neither to the sender's identity/term nor to its configuration membership.

It must come from two things: the request shape restricts which mutations are reachable, and every reachable mutation is taken through a synchronised accessor or a lock-protected field. investigations.discriminator: Enumerate the code reachable for a heartbeat-shaped request and check each mutation's synchronisation (raftState accessors for term/commit/applied, lastLock for snapshot and log indexes, leaderLock for leader address and ID, lastContactLock for last contact, channel sends for observations), then check whether any other producer in the revision can emit an AppendEntries with that same shape while relying on main-loop serialisation. A defect requires an unsynchronised shared field or a producer that can reach main-loop-only state through the fast path; if the classification confines the fast path to the leader's dedicated heartbeat requests and every reachable mutation is lock- or atomic-protected, the concern is refuted at source level, with the residual boundary that an interleaving proof is not attempted.
limitations: Source-only, and deliberately so: the fast path exists only on the network transport (inmem_transport.go:72-76 declines it), and this run's execution isolation has no network namespace, so a network-transport execution is not available in this run.
A local race-detector run of two cluster harnesses was clean, but those harnesses use the in-memory transport, which does not take the fast path, so they say nothing about it.
No interleaving proof is attempted; the assessment covers which mutations are reachable and how they are synchronised.
Observer notification, metrics and stable-store writes reached by a term increase were read but not exercised concurrently.

investigations.question: Does the configuration index exposed by GetConfiguration identify the configuration it returns, and can a caller use that value as the prevIndex guard of a later membership change so that a change is rejected when the configuration has moved on in the meantime?
investigations.hypothesis: GetConfiguration builds its future locally from the atomically published latest configuration and never fills the index field, so ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns the zero value for every caller while Configuration() carries the real membership. The prevIndex guard in nextConfiguration is only enforced when prevIndex is greater than zero, so a caller that passes the returned index is silently unguarded, while the same change guarded with the genuine configuration entry index is rejected once the configuration has advanced.
investigations.discriminator: Read the configuration from the API on each node of a live cluster whose configuration entry index the caller learned from the membership-change future, and compare the returned index with that index; then take an intervening configuration change and retry a guarded change using the value the API returned, with the genuine index as control. A defect needs the returned index not to identify the returned configuration and the guarded change to be applied anyway when the configuration has moved on, while the genuine-index control is rejected; the hypothesis is refuted if the returned index matches the configuration entry index or if the guard rejects the API-derived value.
limitations: Answered: the accessor does not identify the returned configuration and the documented optimistic-concurrency guard cannot be expressed with the value it hands back.

Boundary of the finding: this is a client-contract and concurrency-guard defect, not a consensus-safety defect. Internal configuration tracking used by the main loop comes from a different path and was not shown to be affected, and callers that deliberately pass prevIndex 0 remain unconstrained by design.

The control comparison in the retained receipt came back unknown because the leader-only control event shares one per-node admission alias with three nodes that never produce it; the control's evidence is therefore its retained operand (rejected with 'configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)') rather than a holds outcome.
One node's read was outside applicability because its returned configuration still showed 3 servers at read time, which is why it is absent from comparison 0's evaluated indices.
