knowledge.statement: Raft.timeoutNow performs an unconditional authority transition on the receiver: it clears the known leader, sets the state to Candidate, stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer=true and responds with an empty TimeoutNowResponse. It never inspects the RPC header identity, the current configuration, or any term, and observes no election or heartbeat precondition before transitioning.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to every TimeoutNowRequest that passes checkRPCHeader, delivered to a server in any run state; the request carries only RPCHeader (ProtocolVersion, ID, Addr) and therefore cannot be evaluated for freshness.

knowledge.statement: While candidateFromLeadershipTransfer is set, runCandidate does not pre-vote: it calls electSelf directly, which increments the current term and sends RequestVote with LeadershipTransfer=true. The flag is cleared by a deferred store(false) when the candidate run ends.
knowledge.conditions: Set only by timeoutNow in the captured source; applies to a node that then enters/continues the candidate state.

knowledge.statement: requestVote rejects a vote request that arrives while a different leader is known, but skips that rejection when req.LeadershipTransfer is true; the older-term rejection and the log-suffix comparison still run before a vote is granted.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to RequestVoteRequest handling on any server that has a recorded leader whose address differs from the candidate and whose protocol version carries the LeadershipTransfer flag.

knowledge.statement: The other authority-bearing RPC handlers guard their state change with the sender's term: appendEntries returns early when a.Term is below the current term and only adopts/updates term and state when the request term is greater (or the receiver is not a follower), and installSnapshot ignores a snapshot whose request term is older than the current term.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to AppendEntriesRequest and InstallSnapshotRequest processing; this is the control contrast for the TimeoutNow handler, which has no term to compare.

knowledge.statement: The leader-side leadershipTransfer routine only issues the TimeoutNow RPC after it has driven the target's replication nextIndex past the leader's last log index, i.e. the producer establishes a caught-up target before transferring.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the sender path invoked from leaderLoop; it is not verified by, nor visible to, the receiving timeoutNow handler.

knowledge.statement: GetConfiguration does not read main-thread membership state: it returns a configurationsFuture whose configurations field is filled from the atomically published latestConfiguration, which is written only by setLatestConfiguration (and cleared/initialised elsewhere), so the value a client sees is whatever that atomic last held.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to any caller of GetConfiguration on any server, including followers, independent of the main-thread run loop.

knowledge.statement: Configuration log entries are not delivered to the FSM: the apply loop dispatches only LogCommand to r.fsm.Apply, and for LogConfiguration it calls ConfigurationStore.StoreConfiguration only when the FSM implements ConfigurationStore (otherwise it returns early). MockFSM therefore records only LogCommand payloads in its logs slice and never records a configuration unless the ConfigStoreFSM option is used.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to commit-application in the captured snapshot for every server, regardless of protocol version; Noop and barrier entries likewise never reach FSM.Apply.

knowledge.statement: The captured cluster test helper's EnsureSame compares FSM-applied log payloads and the FSM's recorded configuration list, and its polling limit defaults to 5 seconds (overridden only by a positive MakeClusterOpts.LongstopTimeout). Built with a plain MockFSM and without ConfigStoreFSM, both compared values are empty for a scenario whose only entries are configuration and noop entries, so EnsureSame can pass without establishing that a peer holds the configuration entry.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to clusters created through MakeCluster/MakeClusterCustom without ConfigStoreFSM; the configuration comparison is only meaningful when the FSM implements ConfigurationStore.

knowledge.statement: The appendEntries truncation path is not a mechanism for configurations.latest to stay stale: on a term conflict the conflicting entry is included in newEntries, the suffix is stored, and processConfigurationLogEntry is run for every new entry in the same call, so a configuration entry is (re)applied when it is (re)appended; when the truncated suffix really contained a configuration entry, rolling latest back to the committed configuration is the intended result.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to appendEntries handling of AppendEntriesRequest batches that clear a log suffix at or below configurations.latestIndex.

knowledge.statement: Membership changes are applied with command-specific suffrage rules: AddVoter replaces a non-voter/staging entry with a Voter and only rewrites the address of an existing Voter; AddNonvoter appends a Nonvoter when the server is absent and, when the server is already present with a different suffrage (Voter or Staging), only writes its address while keeping that suffrage; DemoteVoter is the command that turns an existing server into a Nonvoter; RemoveServer deletes the entry. A resulting configuration with no voters is rejected.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to nextConfiguration for a request whose prevIndex matches the current configuration index; the capture's table expectations record the suffrage outcome for each command and initial suffrage.

knowledge.statement: Only some committed log types reach the FSM thread: prepareLog returns a commit tuple for LogBarrier and LogCommand, and for LogConfiguration only when protocolVersion > 2. LogNoop, LogAddPeerDeprecated, LogRemovePeerDeprecated and LogConfiguration under protocol <= 2 return nil, so they never enter the FSM batch; processLogs still responds to any future attached to them from the main thread and then advances lastApplied.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to processLogs dispatching committed entries to fsmMutateCh on the leader and on followers, for every configuration of the FSM (with or without ConfigurationStore and BatchingFSM).

knowledge.statement: The FSM thread's local applied index advances for every entry it receives, except for LogConfiguration when the FSM does not implement ConfigurationStore, where the handler returns early on the stated grounds of not incrementing the index for an unimplemented operation. The index it reports in a snapshot request is that local index, so it can legitimately sit below the committed configuration index.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the single-apply path in runFSM; the batching path instead takes the index and term of the last entry in the batch whether or not it was sent to ApplyBatch.

knowledge.statement: takeSnapshot refuses to create a snapshot when the FSM-reported index is below the committed configuration index, and otherwise records that index/term together with the committed configuration and its index, then compacts only up to min(snapshot index, last log index - TrailingLogs).
knowledge.conditions: Applies to automatic and user-triggered snapshots on any server; the committed configuration is read from the main thread through configurationsCh after the FSM snapshot has been started.

knowledge.statement: A server's reported last log index is max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex), so installing a snapshot raises the server's last index even though appendEntries and installSnapshot do not rewrite the stored log index; installSnapshot updates lastApplied, the last snapshot index, both configurations and log compaction.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to raftState.getLastIndex as used by election and replication bookkeeping and to the InstallSnapshot handler.

knowledge.statement: The automatic snapshot condition compares the log store's last index with the snapshot index using an unsigned subtraction and no ordering guard, so a log store index below the snapshot index makes the comparison permanently true.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to shouldSnapshot as invoked by the snapshot goroutine on its random SnapshotInterval; the log store index is the store's own LastIndex, not the snapshot-aware getLastIndex.

knowledge.statement: A node that recovers through InstallSnapshot while its log store keeps a lower index reports shouldSnapshot() as true indefinitely and keeps creating fresh snapshots at the installed snapshot index while completely idle: in two executions of the same fixed harness the recovered node produced 15 and 13 distinct snapshot IDs at index 202 with applied_delta 0 over a 900ms window (SnapshotInterval 40ms), while the leading node of the same cluster reported shouldSnapshot() false and exactly 1 distinct snapshot ID at index 202.
knowledge.conditions: Observed with MakeCluster(3), SnapshotInterval 40ms, SnapshotThreshold 20, TrailingLogs 5, in-memory log/snapshot stores, protocol 3, after isolating one follower, committing 140 further commands so the leader's log compacts past that follower's next index, reconnecting so the follower recovers by InstallSnapshot (log store last index stays 62, snapshot index 202), then isolating the recovered node for a 900ms window sampled every 40ms. Two executions are instances, not a universal guarantee; MonotonicLogStore implementations, production SnapshotInterval values and long-running persistence were not observed.

knowledge.statement: A verifyFuture can be woken by only one notification (vote is guarded by the notify channel being non-nil and set to nil when it fires), and every respond path is idempotent through the deferError responded flag; vote(true) only notifies once the counted votes reach quorumSize, while vote(false) notifies immediately so the leader loop can step down when any peer reports a new leader.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to VerifyLeader/verifyFuture handling in the captured revision, including the quorumSize==0 dispatch sentinel and the follower/candidate paths that reject arrivals on the shared verify channel with ErrNotLeader.

knowledge.statement: On stepping down, the leader loop responds ErrLeadershipLost to every future still in its own notify set; replication goroutines keep their notify maps separate and only clear them through notifyAll at the end of a replication RPC, so a late notification can push an already-answered verify future back onto the shared verify channel, where the next non-leader loop answers it again through the idempotent respond path.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to leadership loss (step-down, shutdown, or state change out of Leader) with outstanding VerifyLeader requests; the arrivals are handled by whichever run loop is active when they are read.

knowledge.statement: InstallSnapshot validates freshness only by term: an older term is ignored, a newer term transitions the receiver to follower and is adopted, and there is no comparison of the request's LastLogIndex with the receiver's own lastApplied, last snapshot index or log store range. On success the handler restores the FSM from the requested snapshot, sets lastApplied to the request's LastLogIndex, sets the last snapshot index to the request's LastLogIndex/LastLogTerm, replaces both the latest and committed configurations from the request, and then removes all old logs (monotonic stores) or compacts up to the request's index.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to InstallSnapshotRequest handling on any server that reaches the handler, including a server whose own applied index or snapshot index is higher than the request's; the only preceding checks in the handler are the snapshot version bounds and the term.

knowledge.statement: Recovery from a restored snapshot index depends on log replay: processLogs rejects an index at or below lastApplied, otherwise it walks from lastApplied+1 to the target index fetching each log from the store and panics when a needed entry is missing, so a restored index below the previously applied index leaves re-application to entries that must still exist in the log.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to commit-application on any server after a restore, including the install path that sets lastApplied from the request; the walk is bounded by the target commit index and sources entries either from the in-flight future map or the log store.

knowledge.statement: The sender reaches the snapshot path only when it cannot produce entries from its per-peer nextIndex, and nextIndex moves on follower responses: a rejected AppendEntries sets nextIndex to max(min(nextIndex-1, response.LastLog+1), 1), and the snapshot is opened when setupAppendEntries reports the log is not found, i.e. when the needed prefix has been compacted away.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the leader-side replication loop for each peer; the reported last log index used in the backoff comes from the follower's AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog.

knowledge.statement: Across three executions of the same isolation/compaction/reconnect probe on a 3-node in-memory cluster, the node that entered the InstallSnapshot path never reported an applied index below its own maximum: its applied index advanced 27 -> 112 -> 197 -> 257 across rounds with decrease_count 0 and applied_at_end equal to max_applied_seen, while its snapshot index (257) stayed above its surviving log store last index (197) and the two nodes that never entered the install path were monotone as well (snapshot index 257, log store last index 257, decrease_count 0).
knowledge.conditions: Observed with MakeCluster(3), SnapshotInterval 30ms, SnapshotThreshold 10, TrailingLogs 5, in-memory log/snapshot stores, protocol 3, in three rounds of 25 warm commands, isolating one follower, 60 further commands through the remaining quorum, reconnecting, and polling all nodes every 2ms for 1.2s. The probe does not construct a leader snapshot index below a follower's applied index, so this is an observed bounded result and not a guarantee for other configurations.

knowledge.statement: Pipelined replication keeps two separate cursors: pipelineSend advances a private send cursor to the last pipelined entry index + 1 as soon as the request is handed to the pipeline, while the per-follower nextIndex and the commitment map advance only from successful decoded responses (updateLastAppended stores nextIndex = last entry index + 1 and matches commitment, then notifies the verify futures as leader). The decoder aborts the pipeline on the first unsuccessful response, on a newer term (notifyAll(false) plus a step-down notification) and pipelineSend returns shouldStop when setup fails such as a compacted prefix, after which the caller falls back to standard replication or the snapshot path. setPreviousLog additionally special-cases nextIndex-1 equal to the last snapshot index so a snapshot-backed prefix is accepted as the previous log entry.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the leader-side pipeline path in the captured revision for peers that support AppendEntriesPipeline, including the fallback to replicateTo after the pipeline aborts.

knowledge.statement: An incoming AppendEntries is classified as a heartbeat by its field values on the receiving side (non-zero term, a leader address present, PrevLogEntry and PrevLogTerm zero, no entries, LeaderCommitIndex zero). When the transport has a heartbeat handler, it is invoked directly from the connection goroutine and the RPC never reaches the consumer channel; otherwise the request is dispatched to the run loop like any other RPC. The handler registered by Raft is processHeartbeat, which checks shutdown and the command type and then calls the same appendEntries handler the run loop uses.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to NetworkTransport (and to transports that implement SetHeartbeatHandler); InmemTransport declines the fast path and pushes heartbeats onto the consumer channel. The classification depends on request field values, not on an explicit RPC type.

knowledge.statement: For a heartbeat-shaped request the reachable mutations are narrow: the older-term check can return without touching state, a newer term or the sentinel condition sets the state to Follower and adopts the term, the leader address and ID are recorded, and success sets last contact; the previous-log check, the entry loop, configuration processing and the commit-index update are all skipped because PrevLogEntry is zero, there are no entries and LeaderCommitIndex is zero. Each reachable mutation goes through a synchronised accessor (atomic state or lastLock for snapshot/log indexes), leaderLock, lastContactLock, or a channel send for observer notification.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the appendEntries code path when invoked with a heartbeat-shaped request, whether by the transport fast path or the run loop; a request with entries, a non-zero PrevLogEntry or a non-zero LeaderCommitIndex takes the ordinary path and is not covered by this statement.

knowledge.statement: The leader's heartbeat goroutine sends a request carrying only the RPC header, term and leader fields, so its LeaderCommitIndex is zero; on a successful response it refreshes last contact, resets the failure count and notifies any waiting verify futures with the response's success value. Followers therefore learn the leader's commit index from the replicate loop's random CommitTimeout path rather than from heartbeats.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the leader-side heartbeat routine for each peer in the captured revision; the same shape is what the receiving network transport classifies as a heartbeat.

knowledge.statement: GetConfiguration returns a configurationsFuture whose configurations value is built from the atomically published latest configuration only, so Configuration() reports the real membership while Index() reports the zero value for every caller regardless of the configuration entry the value came from. The membership-change guard in nextConfiguration only enforces prevIndex when it is greater than zero, so an index taken from GetConfiguration cannot express the documented condition that the change applies only to the configuration that was read.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to Raft.GetConfiguration on any server and to every membership change command routed through nextConfiguration; the internal configuration tracking filled from the main thread through configurationsCh does carry the index and is unaffected.

knowledge.statement: In a live four-voter cluster whose latest configuration entry index was 3, three nodes returned a configuration with four servers while GetConfiguration's Index() reported 0, so the reported index did not identify the configuration returned by the same call; a membership change guarded with that returned value was applied after an intervening change (entry 4 -> 5), while the same change guarded with the genuine index 3 was rejected with 'configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)'.
knowledge.conditions: Observed in one execution with MakeCluster(3) plus one joining voter through the in-memory transport, protocol 3, reading GetConfiguration on every node after AddVoter returned index 3 and then applying a guarded change; one node's read was outside applicability because it still showed three servers at read time. The values are an observed instance under these conditions, not a claim about internal configuration state.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster; one control RPC (stale-term RequestVote from a non-member claimed sender) followed by one TimeoutNow from the same claimed sender to a follower, with bounded observation of target and leader state/term.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) performs real bootstrap: initial configuration entry, leader election and log replication through the in-memory transport.
Both RPCs are delivered over the in-memory transport with no packet loss, reordering or delay, so any observed transition is caused by the delivered request itself.
The sender identity in the RPC header ('ghost-not-in-config') is deliberately not a configuration member; the probe does not rely on the sender being reachable or registered.
The cluster is healthy before the probe: a leader is serving at a known term, which the harness records as steady_state.
excluded: Network-transport authentication, TLS and peer-identity properties outside the Raft layer.
State-machine safety (log matching, single vote per term) and any claim that the newly elected leader violates it.
Behaviour after the observation interval, further elections, and client-visible unavailability.

parameters.control_request_term: target term at steady state minus 1

basis.prefix: The harness builds the prefix itself with the captured test facilities: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) bootstraps a three-voter configuration through the in-memory transport, waits for a stable leader (c.Leader()), and records the leader id/address/term and the chosen follower's state/term as CA_EVENT steady_state. It then selects the follower's transport peer as sender and emits CA_EVENT control_stale_request_vote after delivering a RequestVoteRequest with Term = targetTerm-1 and RPCHeader.ID = 'ghost-not-in-config'. Only then does it deliver the single TimeoutNowRequest with the same RPC header (no term field exists) and emit CA_EVENT after_timeout_now after a bounded 2s observation of the target and the previous leader. No state is injected and no storage is pre-filled.
basis.requirement: A delivered leadership-transfer order is processed as authority to depose the known leader even though the message carries no term and its claimed sender is not the serving leader or a configuration member; the receiver performs no term, identity or membership check before clearing the leader and starting an election.

Probe: the delivered order moves the follower out of Follower and raises its term, although the order carries no term and its claimed sender is not the leader or a member.
Probe consequence: the previously serving leader is no longer Leader and reports a higher term within the bounded observation interval.

scope.description: One fault-free execution of a normally bootstrapped 3-node in-memory cluster with a small SnapshotInterval/SnapshotThreshold/TrailingLogs: warm traffic, isolation of one follower, further traffic so the leader compacts, reconnection so the follower recovers by InstallSnapshot, then a bounded idle window on the recovered node (isolated again so no further InstallSnapshot can occur) with the leader observed over the same window as control.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3) with SnapshotInterval=40ms, SnapshotThreshold=20, TrailingLogs=5 performs real bootstrap, replication, snapshots and log compaction through the in-memory transport.

Disconnecting only the chosen follower leaves the leader with a quorum (itself plus the other follower), so the cluster keeps committing and the leader's log compacts past the isolated follower's next index.
The isolated follower does not raise its term while isolated because pre-vote is active by default, so reconnecting lets the leader complete the recovery without a spurious election.
Isolating the recovered node again before the window removes the leader as a source of further snapshots, so any new snapshot in that node's store must be produced by its own snapshot goroutine.
Both observed nodes run the same configuration; the leader is idle in the window except for heartbeats.
excluded: Safety claims: no state-machine divergence, lost entry or double application is asserted.
Cost measurement: bytes written, disk wear and FSM Snapshot() latency are not measured.
Behaviour with MonotonicLogStore implementations, which take the removeOldLogs branch instead of compactLogs.
Duration of the condition under production SnapshotInterval values.

basis.prefix: The harness builds the prefix with the captured test facilities and real producers only: MakeCluster(3, conf) with SnapshotInterval=40ms, SnapshotThreshold=20 and TrailingLogs=5 bootstraps the cluster; leader.Apply() commits 60 warm commands so every node snapshots; the chosen follower is cut off with c.Disconnect and 140 further commands are committed by the remaining quorum so the leader's log compacts; c.FullyConnect reconnects and the follower recovers through the InstallSnapshot handler. scope.description: One fault-free execution on normally bootstrapped in-memory clusters: a 3-node cluster plus one joining voter, a configuration read on every node, an intervening membership change, a change guarded with the index the API returned, and a control change guarded with the genuine configuration entry index. excluded: Internal configuration tracking used by the main loop, which is obtained through a different path.
Network-transport behaviour and any transport-level effects.
Performance, and callers that ignore the returned index.

interpretations.rationale: The witnessed conditional execution is the defect: the receiver treats a leadership-transfer order as authority with no term, identity or membership check. Receipt 8248101f2e7e47ecae3104f94cd0357b (completed, exit 0, tests_passed) parsed one test stream of five events. Index 0 steady_state: leader a6e1bccd... in state Leader at term 2, target server-0967aefd... in state Follower at term 2. Index 1 control_vote_sent (claimed_sender_id ghost-not-in-config, request_term 1) and index 2 control_stale_request_vote with rpc_error empty, granted false, target_moved false, target_state_after Follower, target_term_after 2 - comparison_index 0 holds with the control_admission prerequisite matched to index 1, so a request that does carry a term but an older one changes nothing. Index 3 authority_probe_sent (same claimed sender, leader Leader term 2, target Follower term 2) and index 4 after_timeout_now with rpc_error empty, target_state_after Leader, target_term_after 3, target_moved true, leader_state_after Follower, leader_term_after 3, leader_deposed true - comparison_indices 1 and 2 hold with probe_admission matched to index 3. So one delivered TimeoutNow, whose claimed sender is not the serving leader and not a configuration member and which carries no term field at all, moved a healthy follower from Follower to Leader at term 3 and deposed the serving leader inside the 2s observation interval. The source explains why: timeoutNow performs the transition unconditionally (raft.go:2209-2214), the message type has nothing but an RPCHeader (commands.go:206-208), the candidate run skips pre-vote for this flag (raft.go:285-308), and voters then skip the known-leader rejection for the resulting candidate (raft.go:1603-1656), while the producer-side catch-up precondition (raft.go:1003-1032) is invisible to the receiver. The same execution supplies its own control: identical claimed sender, term-carrying request, no movement.

answers.ce1a7dcb68b449448fdee06b3eb7737e-gap-0: Yes, within the executed conditions. In receipt 8248101f2e7e47ecae3104f94cd0357b (exit 0) event index 4 after_timeout_now reports target_moved true with target_state_after Leader / target_term_after 3 (from Follower term 2) and leader_deposed true with the previous leader in state Follower at term 3, after the index 3 authority_probe_sent admission whose claimed sender is not a configuration member; the control event index 2 from the same claimed sender, which does carry an older term, reports granted false and target_moved false. One received TimeoutNow therefore moved a stable follower out of Follower at a higher term and deposed the serving leader, while the stale-term RequestVote left the target unchanged.

knowledge.assertion: timeoutNow clears the leader and enters Candidate without inspecting sender identity, configuration or any term.
the leadership-transfer flag makes the candidate run skip pre-vote and elect at term+1.
voters skip the known-leader rejection when the request carries LeadershipTransfer.

counterevidence: The control shows the term checks used by the vote path do work: the same claimed sender with an older term was refused and changed nothing, so the observed transition is attributable to the TimeoutNow admission path and not to a generally permissive RPC layer.
No safety violation appeared: the target was elected through the normal term/vote exchange, and the previous leader stepped down on the higher term.
limitations: One execution, one fault-free 3-node in-process cluster, in-memory transport; no network-transport authentication, clock or partition conditions are covered.
The deposed leader's client-visible unavailability after the transition is not measured.
The witness does not distinguish a non-member claimed sender from a replayed or delayed order of a legitimate former leader, because the message carries no term to separate them.

interpretations.report_answer: 已确认的缺陷：TimeoutNow 请求只带 RPCHeader、没有任何 term，接收端 timeoutNow 也不检查发送方身份、term 或是否属于当前配置，就直接清除已知 leader、进入 Candidate，并置位 candidateFromLeadershipTransfer。该标志同时关闭两道扰动防护：候选者跳过 pre-vote，投票者跳过“已有 leader 时拒绝投票”。固定输入执行（receipt 8248101f2e7e47ecae3104f94cd0357b，exit 0）中，健康三节点集群里一次来自“非配置成员”声称发送方的 TimeoutNow 使 Follower(term 2) 变为 Leader(term 3)，并迫使原 leader 下台（Follower, term 3）；同一发送方携带旧 term 的 RequestVote 对照未产生任何状态变化。属权威接纳缺陷，不主张状态机安全性被破坏。

interpretations.rationale: No sourced mechanism was established for configurations.latest or the atomically published latestConfiguration being older than a configuration entry the server itself has committed, and the inference that produced the earlier suspicion was corrected by source reading. Configuration entries never reach FSM.Apply (fsm.go:105-118: only LogCommand goes to r.fsm.Apply; LogConfiguration only calls ConfigurationStore.StoreConfiguration when the FSM implements ConfigurationStore), and MockFSM records only LogCommand payloads (testing.go:76-81), so the captured helper's EnsureSame comparison (testing.go:614-676) is vacuous for a cluster whose only entries are configuration and noop entries and cannot show that a peer holds the configuration entry - my earlier claim that the lagging follower had applied the entry while reporting old membership was therefore unfounded. The helper does poll until its limit, which defaults to 5s (testing.go:733-752), so the captured 'peer mismatch' means one node's GetConfiguration read stayed at the 2-server bootstrap configuration for at least the full window while another node reported 3 servers; that is consistent with the entry not having been appended on that node yet, and my instrumented replay of the same scenario (AddVoter of a protocol-3 node into a protocol-2 pair, 250ms polling of configurations.latest/latestIndex and the atomic copy) showed every node converging within 250ms on every run, so no persistent internal divergence was observed. The candidate path named in the earlier hypothesis is also refuted: on a suffix-truncating appendEntries the conflicting entry is included in newEntries and processConfigurationLogEntry is re-run for it in the same call (raft.go:1504-1560), and rolling latest back to the committed configuration after a real truncation is the intended semantics rather than a stale read. The question is left unresolved and paused: the >5s lag itself was not reproduced under instrumentation and its cause (replication scheduling, pipeline state, or something else) is unverified.

answers.ce1a7dcb68b449448fdee06b3eb7737e-gap-1: Not established, with a correction. Source reading shows configuration entries never reach FSM.Apply (fsm.go:105-118) and MockFSM records only LogCommand payloads (testing.go:76-81), so the captured EnsureSame comparison (testing.go:614-676) cannot demonstrate that a peer holds a configuration entry; the earlier inference that a stale-latest node had applied the entry was unfounded. Instrumented replay of the same scenario (protocol-2 pair plus an AddVoter of a protocol-3 node, reading configurations.latest/latestIndex, the atomic latestConfiguration and the log store every 250ms) converged within 250ms on every run, and the appendEntries truncation path re-applies configuration entries in the same call (raft.go:1504-1560), so neither a persistent stale configuration state nor an internal reset behind an appended entry was observed. What remains supported is the weaker observation that in the captured test runs one node's GetConfiguration read stayed at the 2-server bootstrap configuration for the whole 5s EnsureSamePeers window (testing.go:733-752) while another reported 3 servers; whether that was replication lag to that node or a reset was not determined, and no execution was requested for this question.

counterevidence: Local replay of the captured failing scenario converged on every run, so the observed mismatch did not reproduce under instrumentation; it is retained as an unexplained observation rather than as evidence of a defect.
The appendEntries rollback that the earlier hypothesis named is not a stale-latest mechanism: the conflicting entry is re-appended and re-processed in the same call (raft.go:1504-1560).
limitations: No controller execution receipt backs this interpretation; the negative replay result came from a scratch copy of the captured package during exploration.
The captured failing test was observed to fail 2 of 3 isolated local runs before instrumentation; that count is a local observation and not a retained receipt.
Nothing here establishes that a stale configuration state is impossible; it establishes that the specific inference and the specific candidate path were not supported.

interpretations.rationale: The apparent asymmetry is the documented contract rather than a missed demotion. The AddNonvoter documentation (api.go:959-963) states that a server already in the cluster has its address updated, and assigns vote removal to DemoteVoter (api.go:992-996); the AddNonvoter branch (configuration.go:256-276) therefore appends a Nonvoter only when the entry is absent and otherwise rewrites the address while preserving the existing suffrage, and the branch still rejects a configuration with no voters through checkConfiguration. The captured table expectations agree for every initial suffrage: with an existing Voter the expected configuration keeps Voter id1 (configuration_test.go:197-198), with an existing Staging server it keeps Staging (configuration_test.go:199-200), and DemoteVoter on a Voter produces Nonvoter (configuration_test.go:206-207). An operator who wants to take a vote away must call DemoteVoter, so no membership change silently loses or retains authority against the documented contract. Recorded as a source-answered negative result so the asymmetry is not later reported as a defect.
limitations: Source-only: the documentation, branch and captured expectations agree, but no execution was requested and the exact address-rewrite effect was not exercised.
This says nothing about what happens if a DemoteVoter request is accepted while the demoted server is the leader; that path was not investigated.

interpretations.rationale: The lag is real but contained, and the containment is explicit rather than accidental. Committed entries reach the FSM thread only if prepareLog builds a tuple for them (raft.go:1362-1387): LogBarrier and LogCommand always, LogConfiguration only when protocolVersion > 2, while LogNoop and the deprecated peer entries return nil and are never dispatched; processLogs (raft.go:1292-1358) responds to their futures itself and then advances lastApplied. Inside the FSM thread (fsm.go:92-125) every received entry advances the local lastIndex/lastTerm except a LogConfiguration when the FSM does not implement ConfigurationStore, which returns early with the explicit reason that the index should not advance for an unimplemented operation. The snapshot request reports that local index (fsm.go:216-233), so after a committed configuration change with no later command or barrier the FSM index can sit below the committed configuration index. takeSnapshot (snapshot.go:125-211) reads the committed configuration from the main thread afterwards and refuses to snapshot when snapReq.index < committedIndex, with a comment naming exactly this case, so metadata is never labelled with a configuration the FSM has not reached; compaction is separately bounded by min(snapshot index, last log index - TrailingLogs) (snapshot.go:213-240), so nothing beyond the log's last index is trimmed. The observable boundary is that snapshot creation keeps failing with 'cannot take snapshot now, wait until the configuration entry at N has been applied' until an entry the FSM accounts for arrives - and the library's own client contract supplies one, since both a command and a Barrier traverse this path, so the condition is self-clearing under normal traffic rather than a stuck state. No defect is claimed here; the reading explains why the asymmetry between the log index and the FSM index is safe.
counterevidence: The early return would be a silent metadata mislabel if the guard were absent, but snapshot.go:165-176 refuses exactly that case and reports it to the caller, so the weak link identified in the hypothesis is enclosed by a source-visible protection.
Compaction cannot delete past the log head: maxLog is the minimum of the snapshot index and lastLogIdx-trailingLogs (snapshot.go:213-240).
limitations: Source-only: no execution was requested, so this explains the guard rather than observing a snapshot sequence or the error being returned to a client.
The batching FSM path tracks the last entry of the batch (fsm.go:145-171) rather than the last entry sent to ApplyBatch, which was read but not differentially exercised.
Nothing here measures how long a cluster would run without a snapshot in the no-traffic case; the claim is only that the condition is bounded by a legal client operation.

interpretations.rationale: The witnessed conditional execution is the defect: the automatic snapshot condition of a node that recovered through InstallSnapshot is permanently true while the node is idle, so it keeps writing fresh snapshots of unchanged state. Receipt dd59f37872d240548eff168eb821901f (completed, exit 0, tests_passed) parsed five events. Index 0 recovery_state for node server-9f900c62...: the snapshot index advanced from 62 to 202 across the reconnect while the log store last index stayed 62, with log_store_below_snapshot_index true and snapshot_advanced_over_log_store true, i.e. a real InstallSnapshot recovery whose log store was left below the installed snapshot index. Index 1 window_start for that node: should_snapshot true, snapshot index 202, last snapshot index 202, log store last index 62, applied index 202. Index 3 recovered_window_end after 22 samples of 40ms with applied_delta 0: distinct_snapshot_ids 15, snapshot_created_without_new_entries true, newest snapshot index still 202 while the newest ID moved from 2-202-1791708222798 to 2-202-1791708223751, and should_snapshot still true - comparison_index 0 holds with the victim_window admission matched to index 1. The source explains the mechanism: shouldSnapshot (snapshot.go:106-120) compares the log store's LastIndex with the last snapshot index using an unsigned subtraction with no ordering guard, while the snapshot-aware index used elsewhere is max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex) (state.go:159-163); installSnapshot (raft.go:1814-1950) sets the last snapshot index to the installed index and compacts with min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailingLogs) (snapshot.go:216-240), so a node whose log store sits below the snapshot keeps that lower index, and runSnapshots (snapshot.go:72-102) calls takeSnapshot every SnapshotInterval while the condition stays true. takeSnapshot succeeds because the FSM-reported index equals the installed snapshot index, which is not below the committed configuration index (snapshot.go:125-211). In the same receipt the control operands are recorded: index 2 and index 4 for the leader, should_snapshot false with a log store index equal to its snapshot index and distinct_snapshot_ids 1 at index 202 over the same window with applied_delta 0; that comparison's outcome in this receipt is unknown only because the shared end-event name prevented correlation, and the successor harness re-requests it with role-specific event names. Consequence and severity: on a node that recovered by snapshot and then stays idle, the node writes a full-state snapshot every SnapshotInterval indefinitely, with the snapshot store reaping older copies - repeated avoidable IO and FSM Snapshot() work rather than a safety or availability violation.

answers.e2a8cfd757e74ee4965e45968de09795-gap-2: Yes, and nothing in the observed path raises the log store index to prevent the repeat. In receipt dd59f37872d240548eff168eb821901f (exit 0) the recovered node's log store last index stayed 62 while its snapshot index was 202 (event index 0, log_store_below_snapshot_index true), shouldSnapshot reported true at window start (index 1) and still true at window end (index 3), and over the 900ms window with applied_delta 0 the node produced 15 distinct snapshot IDs whose newest index remained 202 - so a fresh snapshot at the same index was created roughly every SnapshotInterval. The leader observed in the same window kept shouldSnapshot false with 1 distinct snapshot ID at the same index 202 (indices 2 and 4). The mechanism is the unsigned delta in snapshot.go:106-120 measured against the log store's own LastIndex rather than the snapshot-aware index, combined with installSnapshot setting the snapshot index above the surviving log store index (raft.go:1814-1950, snapshot.go:216-240) and runSnapshots sampling the condition every SnapshotInterval (snapshot.go:72-102).

knowledge.assertion: shouldSnapshot compares the log store's own last index with the snapshot index using an unsigned subtraction with no ordering guard.
a server's reported last index is max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex), while installSnapshot updates lastApplied, the last snapshot index and compaction without rewriting the log index.
takeSnapshot only refuses when the FSM-reported index is below the committed configuration index, so the recovered node's snapshot at the installed index is allowed.

counterevidence: The control operands recorded in the same receipt show the condition is not universal: the leader in the same window kept shouldSnapshot false, its log store index equal to its snapshot index, and a single snapshot ID at index 202 with applied_delta 0.

The retained receipt's control comparison outcome is unknown (no correlated prerequisite) because both nodes emitted one shared end-event name; this is a harness naming defect in my comparison setup, not a contrary observation, and it is why a successor is requested rather than treated as confirmation.
The node was isolated during the window by construction, so the repeated snapshots cannot be attributed to further InstallSnapshot traffic from a leader.
limitations: One execution, one bounded window; production SnapshotInterval values, larger state, and busy clusters were not exercised.
The measured effect is repeated snapshot creation on a recovered idle node; no state corruption, lost entry or availability failure is claimed, and snapshot retention bounds stored copies.
The witness does not measure the CPU, IO or FSM Snapshot() latency cost of the repeated snapshots.
Monotonic log stores take the removeOldLogs branch instead of compactLogs and were not exercised.

counterevidence: The control comparison now holds against the opposite value: the leader in the same cluster and window had shouldSnapshot false, its log store index equal to its snapshot index, and a single snapshot ID at index 202 with applied_delta 0, so the repeated snapshots are not a property of the configuration or of the window.

The number of distinct snapshot IDs differs between the two executions (15 and 13 over 22 samples at a 40ms interval), which is consistent with scheduling jitter rather than a different mechanism, and is retained here rather than smoothed.
The recovered node was isolated during the window by construction, so the repeats cannot be attributed to further InstallSnapshot traffic from the leader.

Only the in-memory log and snapshot stores with default (non-monotonic) log store behaviour were exercised; MonotonicLogStore takes the removeOldLogs branch instead.
The measured effect is repeated snapshot creation; its CPU, IO and FSM Snapshot() latency cost, and any interaction with slow snapshot persistence, were not measured.
No claim is made that the condition is unrecoverable: any traffic that raises the log store index above the snapshot index ends it, and it is not claimed to affect safety.

interpretations.rationale: The apparent double completion is refuted by completion ownership and ordering. verifyLeader registers the future in the leader loop's notify set and in each replication goroutine's notify map, and the step-down cleanup responds ErrLeadershipLost to everything still in the leader's own set (raft.go:511-526). The replication maps are separate and are only cleared by notifyAll when an RPC finishes (replication.go:100-111), so a goroutine that finishes its heartbeat after the cleanup can still call vote on the same future; vote sends the future onto the shared verify channel and nils its notify channel under voteLock, so it wakes at most once (future.go:272-293). The critical point is who responds: respond is reachable only from the main run loop for this future type (the leader loop's verify branch, the follower and candidate reject branches, and the step-down cleanup), and all of those execute on the single main goroutine, so the cleanup's respond and any later rejection are sequentially ordered rather than concurrent. The second arrival is therefore a no-op: deferError.respond returns early once responded is set, and if it were reached first it would simply answer ErrNotLeader through the same idempotent path (future.go:94-131, raft.go:181-186). The result is that a VerifyLeader outstanding at leadership loss is answered exactly once - ErrLeadershipLost from the cleanup - and any late wake-up on the shared channel is swallowed by the responded flag instead of double-closing the error channel or blocking a sender. A worthwhile boundary follows from the same reading but is not a defect: because vote records a false reply immediately, the leader steps down and answers ErrNotLeader as soon as a single peer reports a new leader, and because votes are only counted from replies, a partition that silences peers leaves the request unanswered until a reply, shutdown or the caller's own timeout resolves it.
counterevidence: The strong form of the suspicion - two concurrent responders racing on the responded flag - requires a respond caller off the main goroutine, and the captured revision has none for verifyFuture: replication goroutines only call vote/notifyAll, which never respond.
The shared verify channel is buffered (api.go:568) so the late notification itself cannot block a replication goroutine.
limitations: Source-only: the ordering argument rests on respond being called exclusively from the main run loop in this revision; a race-detector execution of a concurrent step-down was not requested.
The unresolved-caller-timeout boundary (a verified request that never gets a peer reply) is described, not measured.
No behaviour of other future types or later revisions is claimed.

interpretations.rationale: What is established from source: the receiver's only freshness check is on the term (raft.go:1825-1845), and on success it restores the FSM and then sets lastApplied, the last snapshot index and both configurations from the request before compacting or removing old logs by the request's index (raft.go:1926-1955). The receiver therefore has no index-based defence of its own: if a request whose index is below the node's current applied index were delivered and accepted, lastApplied and the durable FSM state would move backwards, and the only path back is processLogs walking from lastApplied+1 to the next commit index out of the log store (raft.go:1292-1348), which panics rather than silently skipping when an entry is missing. What is not established: whether such a request is reachable. The send-side trigger is narrow - the leader opens a snapshot only when it cannot produce entries from its per-peer nextIndex, and nextIndex only moves on follower responses, with a rejection clamping it to max(min(nextIndex-1, response.LastLog+1), 1) (replication.go:262-300, 355-400). Since a follower reports LastLog = max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex), a follower that has applied beyond the leader's snapshot index also reports a last index at least that high, which makes the decrement path stop at a matching prefix rather than descend past the leader's compacted first index; that argument is plausible but not proven here, and it depends on the follower's log covering its own applied range at the time of the exchange. The concern is therefore recorded as an unresolved boundary with a concrete discriminator instead of a defect: the deciding observation is a delivered InstallSnapshot whose LastLogIndex is below the receiving node's lastApplied while the node's log store first index is above that request index.

knowledge.assertion: the recovered-node state observed in the two executions shows a log store index surviving below an installed snapshot index, i.e. install ordering between the two indexes is a real, observed relation rather than an assumption.

counterevidence: The sender-side backoff uses the follower's reported LastLog, and the reported value is snapshot-aware (max(lastLogIndex, lastSnapshotIndex)), so the leader's nextIndex is pulled down towards that value rather than below it on a rejection; this is the strongest candidate protection against delivering a rewinding snapshot.

A rewind would be re-coverable whenever the surviving log still spans (request index, next commit index], which is the normal case after compaction with trailing logs, so a state regression would have to coincide with a log that no longer covers that range.

interpretations.report_answer: 本场景下的保护成立：固定输入执行（receipt 60a9c1c1920e4c7d9cd3b6c031613b69，exit 0）中，三轮隔离/压缩/重连使 server-9053e19f 进入 InstallSnapshot 路径（index 5 recovery_mode_entered，applied 87、snapshot 87、log store 197 之前的 27），该节点最终 applied_at_end 257 等于 max_applied_seen、decrease_count 0、observed_applied_decrease false，快照索引 257 高于残留日志索引 197；同一窗口内另外两个未进入安装路径的节点同样单调（索引 9、12，applied 257、snapshot 257、日志 257）。两条比较均成立，说明本场景没有出现“快照索引低于接收方已应用索引”的回退安装；源码侧与已记录行为一致：接收端只校验 term（raft.go:1825-1845），发送端把 nextIndex 向跟随者上报的、含快照索引的 LastLog 收敛。未主张缺陷：探针未构造“leader 最新快照索引低于跟随者已应用索引”的配置，因此一般不可达性仍未证明。

interpretations.rationale: The optimistic advance is confined to the pipeline and does not become acknowledged state. pipelineSend builds each request from the current local cursor (setupAppendEntries) and, only after the request is accepted by the pipeline, stores last.Index+1 into that private cursor (replication.go:512-532); the per-follower s.nextIndex and the commitment map are updated exclusively from successful decoded responses through updateLastAppended, which also notifies any waiting verify futures that the leader is still leader (replication.go:534-567, 655-665). Any unsuccessful response stops the decoder, which makes pipelineReplicate return and the replicate loop fall back to standard replication from the last acknowledged nextIndex, so a rejected batch cannot be treated as stored; a newer term additionally notifies the followers' votes as false and signals step-down, and a setup failure in pipelineSend returns shouldStop without sending, which sends the loop back through the standard path where a missing prefix becomes the snapshot path (replication.go:446-510, 224-296). setPreviousLog's snapshot case (replication.go:587-612) covers the boundary where the previous entry is exactly the snapshot index rather than a stored log. No defect is claimed from this reading: the cursor separation plus the abort-and-fall-back rule is an enclosing protection for the concern.
counterevidence: The local cursor is only used to build the next pipelined request; nothing else reads it, so an in-flight NACK cannot promote unacknowledged entries into s.nextIndex or into commitment.
limitations: Source-only; no pipeline failure, out-of-order close or stop-while-in-flight execution was requested.
Assumes the transport pipeline delivers responses in order and reports errors through the same path, which was read but not exercised.

interpretations.rationale: The concern is refuted at source level, with the residual boundary stated explicitly. The fast path is real: net_transport.go:656-690 classifies an AppendEntries as a heartbeat purely from field values (non-zero term, leader address present, PrevLogEntry/PrevLogTerm zero, no entries, LeaderCommitIndex zero), and net_transport.go:718-740 then calls the registered handler in the connection goroutine and jumps straight to responding, so the request never reaches the consumer channel; Raft registers processHeartbeat for that callback (api.go:610-620), which checks shutdown and the command type and calls appendEntries (raft.go:1415-1440). But for that shape the reachable mutations are confined: the older-term branch returns without touching state, a newer term or the non-follower sentinel performs setState(Follower) plus setCurrentTerm, the leader address and ID are recorded, success sets last contact, and the previous-log check, the entry loop, configuration processing and the commit-index update are all skipped because PrevLogEntry, the entry list and LeaderCommitIndex are zero. Every reachable mutation is synchronised: raftState is documented as thread safe and stores term, commit index and applied index atomically with snapshot/log indexes under lastLock (state.go:44-77), the leader address and ID are behind leaderLock, last contact behind its own lock, and observer notifications are channel sends. The classification is also not accidentally reachable from the ordinary replication path in this revision: the leader's heartbeat goroutine deliberately sends only header, term and leader fields with no commit index (replication.go:383-425), while the replicate path sets LeaderCommitIndex to the leader's commit index and a previous log entry once the log is non-empty, so an ordinary AppendEntry cannot take the fast path. Two boundaries remain and are recorded rather than hidden: no interleaving proof is attempted, and the path could not be executed here because the fast path is implemented by the network transport (the in-memory transport explicitly declines it, inmem_transport.go:72-76) and this run's execution isolation provides no network namespace, so my clean local race-detector runs on in-memory clusters do not exercise it.
counterevidence: The narrowness of the fast path is itself the enclosing protection: no field it touches is shared with the main loop without a lock or atomic accessor, and the request shape excludes the paths that mutate logs, configurations and commit state.

The in-memory transport's refusal of the fast path means the cluster harnesses used elsewhere in this run never exercised it, so their clean race-detector results are not evidence about it either way.
limitations: Source-only assessment; no execution of the fast path was possible in this run's isolation (no network namespace) and none is requested.

The classification is value-based, so its soundness depends on producers not emitting that field shape for other purposes; that was checked for the replicate and heartbeat senders of this revision only.
Concurrent observer registration, metrics and stable-store writes reached by a term increase were read but not exercised.
No proof is offered that an interleaving cannot lose a transition; the assessment covers reachability and synchronisation of the mutations.

interpretations.rationale: The registered requirement was violated by the execution: the index that GetConfiguration exposes does not identify the configuration the same call returned, and the documented optimistic-concurrency guard cannot be expressed with it. Receipt 5466e7c2853749f6849e40362a2cdf00 (completed, exit 0, tests_passed) records one config_guard_start admission per node (indices 0-3) with the reference configuration entry index 3, then four config_read results: index 4 (leader server-d2b856e1), index 5 (server-22ab50bc) and index 7 (server-ee231480) each report returned_index 0 with returned_servers 4 and known_entry_index 3, i.e. index_matches_configuration false, which is comparison 0's violation with its guard_start admissions matched at indices 0, 1 and 3; index 6 (server-df765645) reports returned_servers 3 and is correctly outside applicability because that node had not yet observed the new configuration. The control operand at index 10 shows why this is about the returned value and not about the guard: the same kind of change guarded with the genuine index 3 failed with 'configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)'. The source explains the mechanism exactly: GetConfiguration (api.go:895-903) builds the returned configurationsFuture from the atomically published latest Configuration only, so the index field stays at its zero value while configurationsFuture.Index (future.go:255-270) returns that zero to every caller, and nextConfiguration (configuration.go:228-231) only enforces prevIndex when it is greater than zero, so a client that passes the value it was handed silently loses the guard that the AddVoter/AddNonvoter/DemoteVoter documentation describes (api.go:941-957). interpretations.report_title: GetConfiguration 返回的配置索引恒为 0，乐观并发守卫被绕过
interpretations.report_answer: 已确认的缺陷（固定输入执行 receipt 5466e7c2853749f6849e40362a2cdf00，exit 0）：GetConfiguration 返回的 configuration future 只填入原子发布的最新 Configuration，latestIndex 保持零值（api.go:895-903、future.go:255-270），因此 ConfigurationFuture.Index() 对任何调用者都返回 0；而 nextConfiguration 的 prevIndex 守卫仅在 prevIndex > 0 时才生效（configuration.go:228-231），所以调用者用 API 交回的索引做乐观并发保护时会被静默绕过。执行中：配置条目索引为 3 时，三个节点返回 returned_index 0 但 returned_servers 4（index_matches_configuration false，比较 0 违反）；在一次插入的配置变更（条目 4）之后，用以 API 返回值守护的变更仍然成功并写入条目 5（比较 1 违反）；对照中用以真实索引 3 守护的变更被拒绝（configuration changed since 3 (latest is 5)）。结论：客户端契约缺陷（索引不可用于关联与乐观并发），不主张共识安全性被破坏。
